extracted.intended_audience: physicists, students of mechanics, and readers interested in philosophy/epistemology of science
extracted.subtask_description: Normative methodological and epistemological criteria for producing and evaluating scientific theories and expositions in mechanics and physics (e.g., economy of thought, role of cause, experimental foundation, methods of representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The economy of thought is the basis and essence of science; a guiding conception developed from teaching and practical instruction which influences formulation and selection of scientific theories and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach treats economy (mental economy) as a fundamental evaluative principle: it appears in language, mathematics, counting, determinants, calculating machines, Gauss's dioptrics, Newton's Regulae philosophandi, and in the preference for deductions that best satisfy the principle of economy. He explicitly links simplicity and beauty with economy and shows many historical examples where economical formulations are preferred. See references to Gauss, Copernicus, Galileo, Newton, and to his own works (Principles of Heat, Popular Scientific Lectures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as provisional orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of 'cause' has significance only as a means of provisional knowledge or orientation rather than as an ultimate metaphysical grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach follows German philosophical practice distinguishing 'cause' from deeper epistemic grounds; in exact investigations phenomena should be regarded as mutually dependent (like sides and angles of a triangle). Thus invoking 'cause' is acceptable only as an orienting, provisional device, not as an absolute explanatory end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of ideas to facts and to one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific ideas should be adapted to observable facts and to each other; this mutual adaptation is the object of theory-proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach emphasizes beginning with special, definite inquiries and allowing them to act upon the investigator in all phases, ascending from special aspects to more general viewpoints. He cites 'the adaptation of thoughts to one another' (Popular Scientific Lectures) as central to theory construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with the particular and ascend to the general
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodologically, begin investigations with concrete, special phenomena and ascend to general principles rather than attempting a full theory-of-theory at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach argues this approach is practical when indisputable, general, independent truths are not available from which everything can be deduced. He used this method in studying the development of physical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of mathematical representation (calculation reflects thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical steps should transparently express the corresponding steps of thought; symbolic methods should not obscure the reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grassmann's method is praised because 'every step in the calculation is at the same time the clear expression of every step taken in the thought,' avoiding hiding the reasoning behind arbitrary coordinates. Mach contrasts this with common methods that force thought into the background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine analytic and synthetic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, reconcile and combine the advantages of analytic and synthetic approaches rather than privileging one to the exclusion of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach notes Grassmann's procedure (and kindred procedures of Hamilton) removes the difference between analytic and synthetic methods so their advantages are combined; this is presented as a virtue in mathematical exposition and mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and beauty as scientific virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and aesthetic beauty are not merely aesthetic but economical and scientifically valuable criteria guiding theory choice (e.g., Copernicus, Galileo, Newton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach explicitly characterises simplicity and beauty as 'economical' and cites historical examples (Copernicus, Galileo) and Newton's Regulae philosophandi as being substantially influenced by economical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish psychological from logical investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between psychological (how thought develops in minds) and logical (formal analysis) questions when investigating the nature and development of scientific thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach asserts he can and does distinguish these domains, arguing that biological/psychological investigations of thought's development remain necessary even after logical analysis, and that conflating them is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intellectual (thought) experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought experiments (intellectual experiment) are valid investigative tools for examining principles and relationships in science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach lists 'Intellectual experiment' among the productive methods in his inquiry and treats everyday thinking and theoretical constructs as amenable to thought-experiment analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description as a fundamental feature of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear description of phenomena is a fundamental scientific task; accurate descriptive formulation is prerequisite to explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach repeatedly emphasizes the primacy of description (see multiple references in the text/index) and presents exemplars where concise descriptive equations (e.g., simple differential equations) successfully capture phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for simple differential-equation descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing phenomena by simple differential equations is an ideal scientific practice and a mark of close approach to the ideal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach cites Hertz's Investigations on the Propagation of Electric Force (1892) as a good instance where phenomena are described by simple differential equations, illustrating the ideal indicated earlier in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental foundation combined with theoretical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound science combines experimental foundation with rigorous theoretical physical formulation; different contributors may supply distinct but complementary roles (e.g., Mayer philosophical, Joule experimental, Helmholtz theoretical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach stresses that each investigator's contributions (philosophical insight, experimental data, theoretical form) are necessary and complementary in developing robust scientific theory; he uses the historical development of energy theory as example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of conservation principles (principle of energy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles such as conservation of energy are central evaluative and organizing principles for mechanical and physical theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach discusses the history and significance of the principle of energy (conservation) and how it underpins arguments like exclusion of perpetual motion and unique determination relations among mechanical elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on empty maxims; pursue conceptual clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using empty or merely metaphysical maxims ('Out of nothing, nothing comes', 'The effect is equivalent to the cause') as substitutes for demonstrative conceptual clarity and empirical grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach observes such maxims cannot convince and illustrates that Mayer's use of such maxims represented an instinctive yearning later made precise; the caution is to prefer clarity and substantive conceptual work rather than empty aphorisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deductions/ formulations that best satisfy economy
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple systematic deductions or formulations exist, prefer the one that answers best to the principle of economy (i.e., yields simpler, clearer, more unifying presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach notes the same systematic form of a science can be deduced in many manners, but one deduction will correspond better to economy (example: Gauss's dioptrics). This is a criterion for choosing among equivalent formalisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a comparative/ historical perspective in physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative study of different approaches, historical development, and contributions is necessary for a sober and just evaluation of scientific advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach uses comparative presentations (e.g., of Mayer, Joule, Helmholtz) to argue that each made distinctive contributions and that historical/contextual comparison helps evaluate scientific work and avoid over- or under-estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scientific thinking as biological/organic phenomenon where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider everyday thinking and the development of science as biological/organic phenomena, with logical thinking an ideal limit; this perspective is helpful and restraining in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach suggests this viewpoint aids inquiry into adaptation of ideas, mental economy, and the evolution of conceptual frameworks, without denying the value of formal logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy and continuity of thought as methodological aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain constancy and continuity in thought as methodological virtues to keep all conditions of fact constantly before the mind during inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach enumerates 'constancy and continuity of thought' among features helpful in investigating adaptation of ideas to facts, implying disciplined, continuous attention aids in correct theorizing.
